analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Community Reinvestment Act and cuts the corporate tax rate for small locally owned banks.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977, was referred to two House committees and a banking subcommittee in March 1997 and never received a hearing or vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do three things: free banks from the Community Reinvestment Act, the 1977 law that pressures banks to lend in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods; make it explicit that federal credit unions can draw members from multiple groups as long as each group shares a common bond; and cap the corporate tax rate at 15% for small, locally owned lenders that keep most of their loans and shareholders local. It was introduced by Rep. Ron Paul and sent to the Banking and Ways and Means committees, where it died without action.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, especially large ones, would gain by shedding their Community Reinvestment Act obligations. Small, locally owned banks with up to $5 billion in assets would gain a sharply reduced corporate tax rate. Credit unions would gain a statutory guarantee that they can add multiple membership groups, which generally means more people could join and access credit union accounts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, credit unions, and their shareholders

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 outright, removing the federal government's main tool for pressing banks to meet the credit needs of the communities where they take deposits. [S3]

It amends the Federal Credit Union Act so that a federal credit union may be composed of one or more groups, each with its own common bond, ratifying the National Credit Union Administration's practice of permitting multiple membership groups. [S3]

It caps the corporate tax rate at 15% on income above $250,000 (inflation-adjusted) for 'qualified community lenders': insured depository institutions with $5 billion or less in assets, at least 60% local lending, local and individual shareholders, and no publicly traded stock. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, federal taxpayers would bear the cost of the reduced corporate tax rate through lost revenue, and residents of low- and moderate-income neighborhoods would lose the leverage the Community Reinvestment Act gives them when banks want to merge, open or close branches, or redirect lending elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Community Reinvestment Act would end the federal requirement that regulators consider whether banks are serving low- and moderate-income communities, which consumer and community groups have long relied on when challenging bank mergers and branch closures. [S2]

The 15% rate cap is a broad tax cut for an entire class of small banks; because it requires only 60% local lending and $5 billion or less in assets, it would also reward bank owners with lower taxes, with the cost falling on federal revenue. [S3]
The bill combines a major repeal (of the Community Reinvestment Act) with a narrow tax break in a single bill, leaving opponents no way to accept one part without the other. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax cut for small community lenders rewards exactly the kind of local lending the Community Reinvestment Act already encourages, but repealing that law to pay for it would strip away the main federal check on whether banks serve their own neighborhoods. On balance, the bill traded a real protection for lower-income borrowers for a tax benefit to bank owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Banking and Financial Services and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a banking subcommittee a week later, and never moved again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the Financial Freedom Act of 1997 on March 19, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means. [S1][S5]
On March 28, 1997, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit of the Banking Committee. [S5]
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low- and moderate-income communities came out ahead in the narrow sense that the Community Reinvestment Act remained on the books; banks got nothing from this bill, though the credit unions' separate push for membership clarity succeeded through other legislation later in the same Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-income communities kept bank lending rules

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 19, 1997, combining repeal of the Community Reinvestment Act, the credit union membership change, and a reduced tax rate for community lenders. [S1][S3]

for.name: 9 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans. [S4]

against.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: The committee with primary jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Jim Leach (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after sending it to a subcommittee on March 28, 1997; it never advanced. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so the broader partisan split is not visible in the record. [S4]

industries.note: Repealing the Community Reinvestment Act would lift banks' obligation to demonstrate lending in their communities, a gain whose cost falls on lower-income customers. The same bill, however, would ratify expanded credit union membership, which competes with banks — so the bill's main bank-friendly provision is the one that works against the public, and the public-friendly provision works against banks. [S3]

Institutions with $5 billion or less in assets, local lending, and local ownership would see their corporate tax capped at 15% on income over $250,000. The break rewards local lending, but its cost is lost federal revenue and its benefit flows to bank owners. [S3]

The bill writes into law that a federal credit union may combine multiple membership groups, each with its own common bond, letting more people join. Credit unions are member-owned and generally charge lower fees and rates, so this runs alongside ordinary people's interest. [S3]
